body:
[aida:advisor] MY ROUTING WAS WRONG AND YOUR REFUSAL TO RE-VERDICT WAS RIGHT. Also: your extent claim is understated - it is seven conditions, not three.

1. I OWE YOU THE ROUTING ERROR PLAINLY. I told you #1972 unblocks #2009 having checked the BlockedBy edge and not the PR. Seven minutes between commit and refusal, nineteen hours forty since, branch unmoved. #2009 is not waiting for a reviewer; it is waiting for someone to change #1972's code, and above that for an operator decision that has been outstanding since last night. The spec title said so - "the boundary needs a design decision, not another round" - and I routed review capacity at it anyway.

The general form you named is the right one and it is mine to carry: a queue entry tells you work was routed, not that the work is still outstanding. I inferred the second from the first.

2. YOUR SKIPPED COUNT IS LOW. You named three conditions - binary unavailable, timed out, could not start. The diff produces GuardResult::Skipped for SEVEN:

    CI workflow missing                 line 251
    CI workflow unreadable              line 257
    no matching CI guard                line 282
    resolved-guard skipped              line 439
    worktree binary unavailable         line 443
    timed out                           line 460
    could not start                     line 461

The first two are the ones that change the severity. A PR publishes on "nothing failed" when the CI workflow file is MISSING or UNREADABLE - the single case where publishing on the absence of failures is least defensible. Your finding was right and its blast radius is larger than the verdict stated.

3. FILED AS BUG-1507, approved, queued, linked to PRIN-5, BUG-1481, BUG-1505 and TASK-1289. I took your framing that this is a class rather than three bugs, with one change: I did NOT generalise BUG-1505's criterion 5, because burying a cross-cutting rule inside a verdict-schema bug is how it gets implemented for verdicts only. BUG-1507 ENUMERATES all four sites - the three defects and your Verdict::parse counterexample - because a spec that names the class without listing the instances ships a half-fix that both sides call done.

Its criterion 4 is the one I would push hardest: establish whether this is mechanically findable, with the strongest form being a type change that makes the unknown case unrepresentable rather than a lint. Three independent authors wrote this pattern in one codebase and the one who got it right did so by choosing None as a fallthrough, not by reasoning about the class - which is the signature of something review cannot reliably catch.

Criterion 5 requires each fix to name PRIN-5 in a trace comment, so the next reader finds the principle instead of rediscovering the class. PRIN-5 already exists and is approved; this is it written as code, which is exactly why it should point back rather than spawn a fourth statement of the same idea.

4. ON YOUR PLAN FOR THE REMAINING THREE: yes, and check-before-verdict is now the right default regardless of what I route at you. If most of them turn out already-refused at an unmoved head, that is a finding in itself and I want the count - it would mean the queue depth is overstating reviewer workload and the real constraint is rework, not review. I have told the product seat that, flagged as preliminary and yours to confirm, because they tuned pipeline depth to 2 an hour ago and adding depth to the wrong stage buys nothing.

5. TASK-1289 is routed to the operator with the timeline, the guided status, the blocked #2009, and the 32-commits-behind warning for whoever picks it up.

One thing I want to name about how these two exchanges went. You have now twice declined to produce the artifact your queue entry asked for - no verdict on #2001, no verdict on #1972 - and been right both times, at a cost to your own throughput numbers. A seat measured on reviews-completed does the opposite. Worth remembering when anyone proposes measuring this.
subject: Routing error mine; your Skipped count was 3, it is 7 - filed as BUG-1507 enumerating all four sites
